beats.script_body: After a full renovation, the Cooper Hewitt turned the museumgoer from simple viewer into on-the-spot designer. When you enter this handsome museum, you're loaned a whiz-bang electronic stylus and pen. Press the "X"-marked end of the tool to the wall text and you save what you're seeing to a customized website, to learn more later at home — your ticket comes with a personal URL, so you don't have to give up your email or any personal info. The other side of the gadget works as a pen, used at large electronic drafting tables throughout the museum, where what you design can be projected onto the walls around you.

beats.source_passage: When visitors enter this handsome museum (set in a 1902 mansion built for tycoon Andrew Carnegie), they are loaned a whiz-bang electronic stylus/pen to use throughout the visit. Visitors can press the “X”-marked end of the tool to the wall text to save what they’re seeing to a customized website, to learn more about these objects and design later at home (your ticket comes with a personal URL, meaning you don’t have to give up your email address or any other personal info—no privacy worries). The other side of the gadget works as a pen, which visitors use at large electronic drafting tables throughout the museum. In a wallpaper room, for example, what you design at the table (sometimes with the help of historic samples stored in the table’s computer) can be projected onto the walls all around you.

beats.script_body: For decades the beloved Frick Collection has been housed in the ornate neoclassical mansion of Henry Clay Frick, the union-busting industrialist whose sins include partial responsibility for the deadly Johnstown Flood of 1889. Frommer's casts him among history's wealthy sleazeballs — the robber baron who created his own temple of culture. Part of touring the museum was always imagining the lifestyle of the tycoon before his death in 1919.

beats.source_passage: The exceptions are those who created their own temples of culture and learning, like Henry Clay Frick, the union-busting industrialist whose sins include partial responsibility for the deadly Johnstown Flood of 1889. For decades, New York City’s beloved Frick Collection has been housed in the robber baron’s ornate neoclassical mansion at 70th Street and Fifth Avenue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. In addition to seeing the excellent art and furnishings, one of the fascinating aspects of touring the museum was imagining the lifestyle of the tycoon before his death in 1919.

beats.script_body: A long-overdue renovation begun in late 2020 shuttered the Frick mansion for at least three years, moving the collection temporarily a few blocks north to the original building of the Whitney Museum of American Art. With the relocation, the Frick experience becomes less about the man and his mansion and more about the art and artists in the collection — which, Frommer's suggests, may be more appropriate.

beats.source_passage: A long-overdue renovation, however, begun in late 2020, will shutter the mansion for at least 3 years, with the collection moved temporarily a few blocks north, to the original building of the Whitney Museum of American Art. With its relocation, the Frick experience becomes less about the man and his mansion and more about the art and artists in the collection . . . which may be more appropriate.

beats.script_body: Because there is more interior room at the Madison building than at the original mansion, the curators have done something rare in museum land — surfaced the entire collection and devoted entire rooms to just one or two works of art, underscoring which pieces are the Frick's stars. Among them are three of only 34 works Jan Vermeer is known to have painted, plus seminal pieces by Bellini, El Greco, Hans Holbein, John Constable, and J. M. W. Turner.

The layout underscores which pieces are considered the Frick’s stars, allowing visitors to give them the time and attention they deserve. Among those star pieces are 3 of only 34 works Jan Vermeer is known to have painted, plus seminal pieces by Bellini, El Greco, Hans Holbein, John Constable, and J. M. W. Turner, among others.

beats.script_body: The museum's modest goal is to explore 4,000 years of Jewish culture through art. Its two-story permanent exhibition, starting on the fourth floor, gently guides viewers from the biblical era — with its clashes over animal sacrifice and the role of the Temple — through the Diaspora, when the Israelites, forced from their home by successive conquerors, became "wandering Jews," spreading to every part of the known world. What emerges is a portrait of a people who survived against the steepest odds and became magnificently diverse in the process.

beats.source_passage: The “modest” goal of this intriguing museum is to explore 4,000 years of Jewish culture through art. Its two-story permanent exhibition (which starts on the fourth floor) gently guides viewers from the biblical era, with its clashes over such issues as animal sacrifice and the role of the Temple (Jesus wasn’t the only one up in arms over that), through the Diaspora, when the Israelites, forced out of their home by successive conquerors, became “wandering Jews,” spreading to every part of the known world. What finally emerges is a portrait of a people who have not only managed to survive against the steepest odds but have become magnificently diverse in the process.

beats.script_body: The story is told through nearly 800 exquisite artifacts and works of art, with the second half of the exhibit playing almost like a survey of world art styles seen through Jewish eyes. The first- and second-floor galleries host changing blockbuster shows — past ones spotlighting musician Leonard Cohen, artist Marc Chagall, and fashion designer Isaac Mizrahi.

beats.script_body: The Met was founded fairly late, conceived in 1870 by a group of wealthy businessmen and artists. A decade later Calvert Vaux, one of the architects of Central Park, was brought in to create the first red-brick building on this site — you can still see that facade, now the side wall of the European Sculpture Court. A little over a decade later an expansion was needed, so famed architect Richard Morris Hunt was tapped to create the majestic neoclassical Indiana-limestone edifice you see today, awing visitors who climb its mountain of steps and walk past its redwood-height pillars.

beats.source_passage: The Met was founded fairly late, as great museums go, conceived in 1870 by a group of wealthy businessmen and artists. A decade later, Calvert Vaux, one of the architects of Central Park, was brought in to create the first red-brick building on this site (you can see that facade still—it’s the side wall of the European Sculpture Court). A little over a decade later, an expansion was necessary, so famed architect Richard Morris Hunt was tapped to create the majestic, neoclassical Indiana-limestone edifice you see today, awing the visitors who climb its mountain of steps and walk past its redwood-height pillars.

beats.script_body: The Met is the giant among New York museums, figuratively and literally: at 1.6 million square feet it is not just the biggest museum in the city but the largest in the hemisphere — Frommer's argues it competes in stature with the Louvre, the Prado, the Uffizi, and the British Museum. Never a static institution, it now owns more than 3 million works of art spanning 5,000 years, across 18 curatorial departments — from Egyptian mummies to Greek statuary to Islamic carvings to Renaissance paintings to Native American masks.

beats.source_passage: The giant among New York museums both figuratively and literally: At 1.6 million square feet, it’s not just the biggest museum in the city, it’s the largest one in this hemisphere. And I’d argue it competes in stature with the Louvre in Paris, the Prado in Madrid, the Uffizi in Florence, and the British Museum in London. Never a static institution, the museum and its collection have continued to grow, with the Met currently owning more than 3 million works of art spanning 5,000 years. You must choose carefully among the 18 curatorial departments and decide what interests you most. On view are masterworks from nearly all the world’s cultures—from Egyptian mummies to ancient Greek statuary to Islamic carvings to Renaissance paintings to Native American masks to 20th-century decorative arts.

fact_check.notes: Superlative claim ('largest in this hemisphere') — per never-auto-resolve rule, superlatives are not auto-corrected; left to /fact-check.

beats.script_body: On the second floor, the European paintings collection encompasses some 700 works. Its jewels include Velazquez's truer-than-life portrait of Juan de Pareja — the enslaved man whom the painter respected enough, as you can see in the painting, to set free; El Greco's brooding landscape of Toledo; 20 Rembrandts, among them Aristotle Contemplating the Bust of Homer, where Alexander the Great's pendant hangs from Aristotle's shirt; five light-kissed Vermeers; and a roomful of van Goghs.

beats.script_body: The Egyptian Collection includes pieces discovered by the Met's own teams of archaeologists, such as miniature figures from a tomb in Thebes that show in intricate detail what daily life was like for a wealthy Egyptian. Its centerpiece is the Temple of Dendur, an actual temple to the goddess Isis dating to about 15 b.c. that was saved from the rising waters of the Nile after the construction of the Aswan Dam.

There’s also elaborate statuary; mummy cases; jewelry; wall paintings; and the Temple of Dendur, an actual temple to the goddess Isis (ca. 15 b.c.) that was saved from the rising waters of the Nile after the construction of the Aswan Dam.

Most stunning is the Cubiculum from Boscoreale, a perfectly preserved, brilliantly colorful room from a villa near Pompeii that was buried when Mount Vesuvius erupted in a.d. 79.

beats.script_body: On Friday and Saturday evenings the Met stays open late — not just for art but for cocktails on the roof and in the Great Hall Balcony Bar from 4 to 8:30pm, where classical music from a string ensemble accompanies the tippling. The Petrie Court Café and Wine Bar serves dinner with piano music until 10:30pm. Best of all, the crowds dwindle after dark in the galleries, if not near the bars.

beats.script_body: Thanks to a 2016 overhaul, this century-old museum, founded in 1923, finally makes good on the promise of its name. It offers a textured, dramatic look at the improbable tale of a tiny, obscure Dutch colony that blossomed — and burned, and conned, and fought — into a world capital. Start in the basement, where a 30-minute film narrated by Stanley Tucci outlines the story, then move to the ground floor, where a gallery traces Gotham's history from Native American days through the 1900s, with electronic panels profiling New Yorkers from Alexander Hamilton to a murdered prostitute.

beats.source_passage: Thanks to a 2016 overhaul, this century-old museum (founded in 1923) is finally making good on the promise of its name. Today, it offers visitors a textured, dramatic, suavely interactive look at the improbable tale of a tiny, obscure Dutch colony that blossomed—and burned, and conned, and fought—into a world capital. Start your visit in the basement, where an absorbing 30-minute film (narrated by Stanley Tucci) outlines the story. Next stop should be ground floor, where one gallery traces Gotham’s history from Native American days through the 1900s, displaying artifacts of all sorts, accompanied by electronic panels offering biographies of New Yorkers both well-known and obscure—everyone from Alexander Hamilton to a murdered prostitute—that illuminate different strands of the story.

beats.poi_name: Museum of the City of New York
beats.script_body: On the ground floor, the Future City Lab lets visitors try to solve the city's problems — sustainability, population density and the rest — on individual tablets that are later screened for all to see. Upstairs are changing exhibits, a famed dollhouse, galleries of Gilded Age frippery, and an excellent permanent exhibition on activism in NYC.

beats.script_body: The Neue Galerie offers a swift but effective overview of German and Austrian arts and design. It is most notable for its jewel-toned paintings by Gustav Klimt — including the famed Woman in Gold — its "Didn't I sit on that in the '70s?" Bauhaus furniture, and its collection of drawings by Teutonic masters such as Dix, Schiele, and Breuer. Because some of those drawings are a bit racy, children 11 and under are not admitted.

beats.source_passage: Most notable for its jewel-toned paintings by Gustav Klimt (including the famed Woman in Gold), its “Didn’t I sit on that in the ’70s?” Bauhaus furniture, and its collection of drawings by such Teutonic masters as Dix, Schiele, and Breuer, the Neue Galerie offers a swift but effective overview of German and Austrian arts and design. Because some of these drawings are a bit racy, children 11 and under are not admitted, and ages 16 and younger must be accompanied by an adult.

beats.script_body: New York is the city of the rectangle and the sharp right angle — our streets a grid, our buildings boxy and regular — until you get to the Guggenheim. Frank Lloyd Wright's delirious spiral of a museum sits among the towers of Fifth Avenue like a steroidal peacock among guinea hens. Critic Herbert Muschamp described it best: "What else but a building brought back from a dream would be windowless, have walls and floors that tilt and twist, begin on the top floor, and spiral in towards the center like an enigma?" Visiting this 1959 masterpiece and trudging up the ramps of its curving halls turns the standard museum experience into a profound journey — and sometimes a battle against vertigo.

beats.source_passage: New York is the city of the rectangle, of the sharp right angle. Our streets form a grid, our buildings are boxy and regular. Until you get to the Guggenheim, that is. Frank Lloyd Wright’s delirious spiral of a museum sits among the towers of Fifth Avenue like a steroidal peacock among guinea hens. Architectural critic Herbert Muschamp described the look best when he wrote, “What else but a building brought back from a dream would be windowless, have walls and floors that tilt and twist, begin on the top floor, and spiral in towards the center like an enigma?” Visiting this 1959 masterpiece and trudging up the ramps of curving halls transforms the standard museum experience into a profound journey (and sometimes a battle against vertigo), no matter what art is displayed.

beats.script_body: Early critics dismissed the Guggenheim — Newsweek's insipid review was headlined "Museum or Cupcake?" — yet Frommer's argues even the most jaded visitor today feels the power of the place, the symbolic weight of infinite circle upon circle. And to answer the question nobody ever voices aloud: no, there have been no suicide jumps from over the low-slung rails, nor has anyone ever accidentally fallen to their death.

beats.script_body: Beyond its architecture, the Guggenheim is popular for its curators' skill at mounting blockbuster retrospectives on top contemporary artists like Robert Mapplethorpe, Cecilia Vicuña, and Gillian Wearing, and shows that combine art with history and sociology. Permanent gallery space is given to the stars of its collection — towering modernists such as Chagall, Brancusi, Mondrian, Miró, and Kandinsky.

beats.source_passage: Beyond the architecture, the museum is popular, thanks to its curators’ skill at mounting blockbuster retrospectives on top contemporary artists (like Robert Mapplethorpe, Cecilia Vicuña, and Gillian Wearing) and topics that combine art with history and in some cases sociology—shows on contemporary Middle Eastern and North African art, Aztec culture, the photography of motorcycles, to mention just a few that created headlines in past years. Permanent gallery space is also given to the stars of the Guggenheim’s collection, towering figures such as Chagall, Brancusi, Mondrian, Miró, Kandinsky, and other modernists.

beats.script_body: Since 1869 this institution has been both the country's preeminent private scientific research facility and its top museum for paleontology, zoology, anthropology, and now astronomy — and the flow between its research and curatorial sides keeps it fiercely vital. A few years ago scientists concluded that dinosaurs had not dragged their tails as long thought but waved them in the air as they walked. The curators responded by painstakingly dismantling the famed dino skeletons and reassembling them with tails erect, then placed one skeleton atop a section of a Texas riverbed where they had found fossilized dino footprints with no tail-dragging marks — a peephole into how scientific theories emerge.

beats.source_passage: Since 1869, this institution has served as both the country’s preeminent private scientific research facility and its top museum for paleontology, zoology, anthropology, and, in recent years, astronomy. Just a few years ago, for example, scientists concluded that dinosaurs had not dragged their tails as had long been thought but waved them in the air as they walked. The curators responded, painstakingly dismantling the museum’s famed dino skeletons and reassembling them with tails erect. Then, in a brilliant stroke, they placed one skeleton atop a section of a Texas riverbed where they had found fossilized dino footprints (sans tail-dragging marks), giving museumgoers a peephole into how scientific theories emerge.

beats.script_body: In 2023 the $431-million Richard Gilder Center for Science, Education and Innovation opened, transforming the museum-going experience. Its new 230,000-square-foot structure houses 12% of the museum's collections, including an insectarium, a permanent butterfly vivarium, open storage exhibits, and a 360-degree Invisible Worlds Theater about the networks that underlie all life. Be sure to enter through this new center: the dazzling lobby mimics curving Southwestern American canyons, a sinuous look created by spraying structural concrete directly onto rebar.

beats.source_passage: That effort became even more cutting-edge in 2023, when the $431-million Richard Gilder Center for Science, Education and Innovation opened, transforming the museum-going experience. It houses 12% of the museum’s collections in a new 230,000-square-foot structure including an insectarium, a permanent butterfly vivarium, open storage exhibits showing the span of the museum’s collections, and a 360-degree-view Invisible Worlds Theater, a mesmerizing high-tech show about the networks that underlie all life (it’s hard to describe, but a real wowzer of an experience). Be sure to enter the museum through this new center: The dazzling, contemporary architecture of its lobby mimics curving Southwestern American canyons, a sinuous look created by spraying structural concrete directly onto rebar.
